entries.description:
The Syntax Helper exposes every language keyword, built-in function, primitive type, and metadata accessor available inside an OES configuration. It is read-only documentation that lives alongside the editor — it never modifies your configuration on its own.

Three tabs cover three navigation patterns. Contents groups entries by category. Index lists every name alphabetically with prefix-search. Search runs a token query across names + signatures.

Use the toolbar Back / Forward buttons to retrace your steps, Reload to pull in newly added help files without restarting, Sync to look up the identifier under the editor caret, and the Larger / Smaller text buttons to scale the description font. Press RawCtrl+F1 (Ctrl+F1 on Windows / Linux) in the editor to open the helper on the identifier under the cursor; RawCtrl+Alt+F1 toggles the pane.

Drag-and-drop: pick an entry in the Index or Search list (or the Contents tree) and drag it into the editor — the matching syntax template inserts at the drop position. The template respects the active compile mode (CES braces vs VES End* terminators).

entries.signature: from <item> in <source> [where ...] [orderby K1[, K2...] [ascending|descending]] [group ... by ... [into ...]] select ...
entries.description:
LINQ — language-integrated queries against in-memory collections. Two parallel surfaces compile to the same primitives.

**Block syntax** (eager): `from <var> in <source>` opens the query; `where / var / orderby K1[, K2...] [asc|desc] / group X by K [into g] / join b in Y on a.K equals b.K / skip N / take N / distinct` clauses; closes with `select <expr>` or `select { F = expr, ... }`. Materialises to an Array immediately.

**Chain syntax** (lazy): `arr.Where(λ).Select(λ).Distinct().Take(10).ToArray()`. 31 operations available — pipeline (Where / Select / Distinct / OrderBy / OrderByDescending / GroupBy / Join / Skip / Take / SkipWhile / TakeWhile / Reverse / Concat / Union / Intersect / Except / WhereIndexed / SelectIndexed), terminals (Count / ToArray / First / Last / Single / Any / ElementAt / Contains / SequenceEqual / Aggregate plus *OrDefault variants), aggregations (Sum / Min / Max / Average — with optional lambda selector).

Lambdas close over outer-scope locals: `var k = 5; arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > k; })`.

LINQ keywords compile identically in CES and VES modes.
entries.syntax_block:
var q = from o in orders
        where o.Total > 100
        var doubled = o.Total * 2
        orderby o.Warehouse, o.Date descending
        select { N = o.N, V = doubled };
entries.return_descr: Array of selected rows (block syntax) or lazy iterable (chain syntax).

entries.description:
A FUNCTION CAN BE A VALUE. `Function(x) { return x * 2; }` written where a value is expected produces a callable that can be stored, passed, returned and called later. Same keyword as a declaration; what makes it a value is the position it stands in.

WHAT THEY ARE FOR — three jobs, and finding yourself in one of them is how to know a lambda is wanted:

1. A CALLBACK — work handed to somebody else to run: `arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > k; })`. The collection decides WHEN to call it and with what; you only say what to do with one element.

2. AN EVENT HANDLER — behaviour attached to something that will happen later, without declaring a named procedure for it.

3. A RULE PASSED AS AN ARGUMENT — a comparison, a filter, a projection given to a routine that would otherwise be fixed: `Function Apply(f, v) { return f(v); }`.

THEY REMEMBER WHERE THEY WERE WRITTEN (closure). A lambda reads the locals around it — of the procedure and of the module — and reads them AT CALL TIME, not when it was written:

    var n = 1;
    var f = Function(x) { return x + n; };
    n = 100;
    f(0)   // 100

A parameter of the same name shadows the captured one, and the outer value is left untouched.

CALLING ONE THAT LIVES IN A CONTAINER GOES THROUGH A VARIABLE: `s.f(1)` and `a[0](1)` do not compile, while `var g = s.f; g(1)` does.

⚠ DO NOT REACH FOR A LAMBDA WHERE A CLAUSE SAYS IT SHORTER. Filtering, projecting, sorting and grouping a collection are written with KEYWORDS, and every lambda those would need is text you do not have to write:

    from x in arr where x > limit select x                      // short
    arr.Where(Function(x) { return x > limit; }).ToArray()      // the same thing, twice as long

Keep lambdas for the three jobs above — a callback, a handler, a rule handed to somebody else. See guide.linq for the clause order.

entries.name_local: JSON — reading and writing (JSONReader, JSONWriter, JSONValueType, JSONFormatting)
entries.name_en: JSON — reading and writing (JSONReader, JSONWriter, JSONValueType, JSONFormatting)
entries.description:
JSON FROM A SCRIPT - an exchange with a cash register, a marketplace, a bank. Two types, reading apart from writing; the kinds of things are said with system enumerations, not numbers or strings.

READING THE WHOLE VALUE - `ReadValue()`. An object becomes a `Structure` (its keys may be ANY strings and keep the order they came in: `s.name` for a key that is a name, `s["odd key"]` for one that is not), an array an `Array`, `null` is `Null`, the rest are String, Number, Boolean. A key met twice keeps its LAST value. ONE THING A Structure CANNOT HOLD: two keys that differ only in case - its keys fold case and JSON's do not - so `ReadValue()` REFUSES such an object by both names rather than merge them; walked with `Read()` it reads like any other.

A NUMBER IS READ FROM ITS TEXT, NOT THROUGH A double. `0.1` in a message is one tenth, and `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.3` - money that came through a binary fraction no longer adds up. Every digit arrives as written - within limits that are said, not met by surprise: a magnitude past about 1e308, a number longer than a thousand characters or an exponent beyond a thousand is REFUSED, never rounded. `JSONWriter` writes a number the same way.

TOKEN BY TOKEN - `Read()` steps to the next token and answers False when nothing is left; `CurrentValueType` is a `JSONValueType` (`None`, `Null`, `Boolean`, `Number`, `String`, `PropertyName`, `ObjectStart`, `ObjectEnd`, `ArrayStart`, `ArrayEnd`), `CurrentValue` is the name or the scalar. `ReadValue()` hands over the whole value the reader STANDS ON; standing on a property name - or before the first token, or on a value already taken - it is the value that FOLLOWS. So a member's value is `ReadValue()` right after its name, and the elements of an array are taken one at a time: `Read()` to the next token, stop at `ArrayEnd`, else `ReadValue()`. `Skip()` steps over a container, or over a property together with its value.

A TEXT THAT IS NOT JSON IS REFUSED WHEN IT IS GIVEN - whole, with the line and column - not after the script has acted on its first half. Something after the value, a trailing comma, single quotes: all refused.

WRITING - `WriteStartObject` / `WriteEndObject`, `WriteStartArray` / `WriteEndArray`, `WritePropertyName(name)`, `WriteValue(value)`, and `Close()` hands over the text. The global functions `ReadJSON(reader)` and `WriteJSON(writer, value)` are the reference system's spelling of `ReadValue()` and `WriteValue(value)`. `WriteValue` takes a String, a Number, a Boolean, a Date (ISO 8601, `2026-09-20T21:05:39`; an empty date is `null`), `Null` and `Undefined` (`null`), and a Structure / Container / Array of those to any depth. The writer keeps the document well-formed by itself: a value inside an object needs its name first, an end closes what was opened, a document holds ONE value, `Close()` refuses while anything is open or when nothing was written - each is an error that says which. `JSONFormatting.Indented` puts a member on a line; `Compact` (the default) is one line.

WHAT HAS NO JSON FORM IS REFUSED BY NAME - a reference, a table, an enumeration member. What stands for it in the other system (a code, a description, a Guid) is the exchange's decision: write that. A refused value leaves nothing of itself in the text.

The text is a string: a file is the business of whatever reads and writes files.

entries.name_local: Declared types — say what a parameter or a variable takes
entries.name_en: Declared types — say what a parameter or a variable takes
entries.description:
THE TYPE STANDS BEFORE THE NAME: `Procedure OnClick(AnyControl element)`, `Array rows;`. It is optional - no type means anything - and it is WRITTEN FOR THE READER: whoever researches the code, a person or an assistant, sees what a routine takes without reading its body, and a type name that does not exist is a compile error rather than a surprise at run time. So declare the parameters of anything written for others to call.

WHAT CAN BE DECLARED:

- the primitives: `Number`, `String`, `Date`, `Boolean`;
- a value class by its registered name: `Array`, `Structure`, `Table` (the value table)…;
- a FAMILY - a filter that creates nothing, and lets a whole kind through, members added tomorrow included:
    `Any` - anything, said rather than left unsaid
    `AnyRef` - any reference (catalog, document, chart…)
    `AnyObject` - any data object
    `AnyManager` - any manager
    `AnyControl` - any form control
    `AnyValue` - any general-purpose value (array, structure, value table)
    `AnyEnum` - any enumeration
    `CatalogRef`, `DocumentRef`, `ChartOfAccountsRef`… - any reference OF ONE METATYPE, whichever object.

EMPTY ALWAYS FITS. A parameter nobody passed or a reference not filled in is the empty value: the declaration says what the value IS when there is one, not that there is one.

WHAT DOES NOT WORK YET (measured 2026-09-15):
- `Val` together with a type - `Val Number n` does not compile. A typed parameter is written without `Val`.
- one configuration object's reference, `CatalogRef.Goods item` - declare the family (`CatalogRef item`) and let the name say which catalog.
- the editor's completion does not read a declared type yet; the declaration serves the reader and the compiler.

`type_list` (the assistant's tool) answers which type names exist.

entries.name_en: Cached functions — an answer used again (settings, the policy for a period)

entries.name_local: Entering on the basis — one object made from another (an invoice from an order)
entries.name_en: Entering on the basis — one object made from another (an invoice from an order)
entries.description:
ONE OBJECT ENTERED FROM ANOTHER - an invoice from an order, a payment from an invoice - is three pieces the platform already has. Nothing is written but the filling itself.

1. WHAT MAY BE ENTERED FROM WHAT is a binding on the SOURCE: its `ListGeneration` property lists the kinds that can be made from it (the designer's property grid, or `metadata_bind` with `ListGeneration`). Empty: nothing is entered from it.

2. THE PERSON presses the standard *Generate* command of the source's form. It offers exactly the kinds in that list, creates the chosen one and opens its form.

3. THE NEW OBJECT FILLS ITSELF, in its own object module, in the handler `Filling(Source, StandartProcessing)`. `Source` is the reference it was entered from - the order. The same handler runs for a plain new object too, with `Source` empty - that is where its defaults go - so the first lines of the handler tell the two apart. Setting `StandartProcessing = False` REFUSES the entry: the object is not created and no form opens. Use it when this source cannot give such an object (an order already closed).

FROM CODE the same filling is asked with `Fill`: `var doc = Documents.Invoice.CreateDocument(); doc.Fill(order); doc.Write();` - the new object's own `Filling` runs with that source. So the rule lives in ONE place, whether a person or a routine enters the object.

WHAT TO CARRY OVER is craft, not mechanism - the pattern `entered-from` (pattern_read): attributes of the same name carry over; the rate, the currency of a till and the number are worked out afresh for the new document; lines are filled from what is STILL OUTSTANDING on the source (`document-chains`), not copied from its lines as written.
entries.parameters: Source - the reference the object is entered from; empty for a plain new object. StandartProcessing - True on entry; set it to False to refuse creating the object.

entries.name_local: Subordinate catalogs — items that live with an owner (units of an item, contracts of a counterparty)
entries.name_en: Subordinate catalogs — items that live with an owner (units of an item, contracts of a counterparty)
entries.description:
A CATALOG WHOSE ITEMS BELONG TO AN ITEM OF ANOTHER - the units of measure of a product, its characteristics, the contracts or bank accounts of a counterparty - is declared in METADATA, not written in code. The subordinate catalog's `ListOwner` names the catalogs that own it: the designer's property grid, `metadata_bind` with `ListOwner`, or `ListOwner` among `metadata_create`'s properties. Like any catalog it may be hierarchical as well.

WHAT IT GIVES:
- every item and folder gets the predefined attribute `Owner`, typed by that list - a reference to the owner's item (several owner catalogs make it a composite type);
- `Owner` is REQUIRED: an item without one is refused on write;
- `Owner` is an ordinary column - `SELECT ... FROM Catalog.Units WHERE Owner = &Item`, and in LINQ `From u In Data.Catalogs.Units Where u.Owner = item`.

WHEN: the thing makes sense only with its owner - units, packings, characteristics, contracts, a counterparty's bank accounts. What many owners share (a currency, a warehouse) is not subordinate.

HOW IT BEHAVES FOR THE PERSON. A subordinate list is shown for ONE owner, and a choice on a document line offers only the items of the line's owner - a contract of the document's counterparty, a unit of the line's product. That is the point of subordination, and it is the PLATFORM's to do, by the owner - not each configuration's. So when building a configuration, LOOK whether the list and the choice are narrowed; where they are not, that is a requirement to raise with the platform's owner, not a workaround to write into every form. A QUERY is another matter: it reads what it is asked, so a query over one owner's items filters by `Owner` itself.

entries.name_local: Files — reading and writing text, and bytes as they are (TextReader, TextWriter, BinaryData, TextEncoding)
entries.name_en: Files — reading and writing text, and bytes as they are (TextReader, TextWriter, BinaryData, TextEncoding)
entries.description:
THE CONTENT OF A FILE, FROM A SCRIPT. `File` answers whether a file exists and how large it is; these read and write what is in it - an exchange file of another system, sales out of a cash register, a price list - on every platform, with no COM object in between.

TEXT, LINE BY LINE - `TextReader`. `ReadLine()` hands over the next line WITHOUT its line break (CRLF and LF alike); `Read()` hands over everything that is left as one text; `Close()` lets the file go. THE END OF THE FILE IS `Undefined`, NOT AN EMPTY STRING: an empty line is a line, and a loop written against `""` stops at the first blank line of the file - or, written the other way round, never stops.

BY NUMBER - `LineCount()` is how many lines the file has, `GetLine(n)` is line n counted FROM ONE: the very lines `ReadLine()` hands over, cut the same way, and neither moves where `ReadLine()` is. A line break at the very end of the file ENDS the last line rather than opening an empty one after it: a file of `"a"` + LF is ONE line, where `StrLineCount`, which counts a text, says two. No such line is `Undefined`, as the end of the file is for `ReadLine()`.

WRITING - `TextWriter`. `Write(text)` writes the text as it is, `WriteLine(text)` adds ONE line break - LF, the same on every platform, so a file written here reads the same there. The third constructor argument, `True`, APPENDS to the file instead of replacing it. A writer nobody closed still leaves its text on disk, but close it: the file stays open until then.

THE ENCODING is said with the `TextEncoding` enumeration - `UTF8` (when left out), `UTF16`, `ANSI` and `OEM` (the code pages of the machine the platform runs on, asked of the system), `System`. A byte-order mark at the head of a UTF-8 or UTF-16 file is read as a mark and never handed over as text; a UTF-16 mark also says which byte comes first. On writing, UTF-16 gets its mark and UTF-8 does not. Bytes that do not spell text in the encoding given are an ERROR, not a text with holes in it - so is a file that cannot be opened, and the message names the file.

BYTES - `BinaryData`. `Read(path)` takes the file's content whole, `Write(path)` puts the content into a file, `Size()` is the number of bytes. A string handed to the CONSTRUCTOR still means base64, not a path - which is why reading a file is a method.

The whole file is decoded when it is opened: these are for exchange files, not for logs of gigabytes.
